newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Row over Spratlys cools Manila-Beijing romance.
newsitem.headline: Row over Spratlys cools Manila-Beijing romance.

text.p: They appeared to be bosom friends as they went sailing on Manila Bay in November, dancing the waltz and crooning a duet of "Let Me Call You Sweetheart".

But six months after Chinese President Jiang Zemin met his Philippine counterpart Fidel Ramos the romance between Asia's giant and its puny neighbour has cooled, their relations now dogged by suspicion and mistrust.

On Monday, Philippine and Chinese foreign ministry officials will meet in Beijing to try and defuse tension brought about by their competing claims over a cluster of bleak islets and rocks in the South China Sea.
"What we will tell them is let us not make the fire bigger," Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said on Sunday.
The long-standing row over the Spratly Islands and nearby shoals and reefs flared anew last month when Manila accused Beijing of sending armed naval ships into areas Filipinos occupy.

Days later, Philippine naval vessels drove away a Chinese-organised expedition of radio hams from Scarborough Shoal, north of the Spratlys, and allowed fishermen to hoist the Philippine flag over the Chinese-claimed rocks.
Beijing has insisted the Spratlys and other islands in the South China Sea historically belongs to it, saying its claim dates back to the Han dynasty between 206 B.C. to 220 A.D.

Straddling vital sealanes and believed to sit atop vast reserves of oil and natural gas, the Spratlys comprise about 200 islets, reefs and shoals which are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.

Jiang pledged in talks with Ramos in November that China would not be a threat to any country. They sealed the pledge with a cruise on Ramos's yacht where they danced and sang "Let Me Call You Sweetheart" and the Elvis Presley hit "Love Me Tender" from a song book titled "Sailing Together to the 21st Century".

Last month Ramos was singing a different tune. Speaking during a visit to the United States, he said the Spratlys dispute "is for us the litmus test of whether China intends to play by international rules or make its own".
Philippine Senate foreign relations committee chief Blas Ople said: "While Jiang and Ramos were carousing, our good friends, the Chinese, were grabbing our territory in the South China Sea."

"China is approaching its international relations from a Marxist viewpoint," political analyst Carolina Hernandez said. "On the one hand, it talks to us nicely ... at the same time it is making its creeping occupation of islands we claim."
Analysts said the Philippines was an ideal testing ground for Chinese probing, being one of the weakest members militarily of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
"I think what China is doing is probing to what extent the coherence and cohesion (of ASEAN) will remain," Hernandez said.

Manila enjoyed the U.S. protective umbrella until 1992 when Washington closed down Subic naval base -- 200 kms (125 miles) east of Scarborough Shoal -- after Manila rejected a new bases pact with its former colonial master.
Now, Philippine senators are proposing that U.S. Navy ships be allowed back into Subic to resupply and refuel.
"They would present a countervailing force to Chinese threats," Ople said.
Some diplomats are not overly alarmed by developments, saying they thought Manila might be playing up the incidents to justify a bigger military budget so it could replace its navy's decrepit fleet.
Political analyst Amando Doronila described the Spratlys dispute as "a powder keg" and accused China of "probing weaknesses and the will of rival claimants who might be intimidated by its size".
"Filipinos -- the hot-headed Latin-types of Southeast Asia -- are not easily cowed by Chinese bullying," he added.
